analysis.one_liner: Funds 12 million new public and affordable housing units over a decade.
analysis.headline: The Homes for All Act, backed by 10 House Democrats, never received a hearing, markup, or vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created 9.5 million publicly owned housing units and 2.5 million affordable private-market units over 11 years, repealed the federal ban on building new public housing, permanently funded public housing operating and repair costs, and sent $200 billion to cities to fight gentrification and displacement. It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where no action was ever taken on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Very low-income and severely cost-burdened renters — the bill's own findings say more than 18 million households pay over half their income for housing — would gain access to publicly owned, permanently affordable homes that cannot be sold off, along with protections against discrimination based on criminal record or immigration status.

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes $80 billion per year from FY2022 through FY2032 to build new public housing units, which the bill's purpose clause sets at 9.5 million units over 10 years, and bars their sale during their useful life.
Repeals the Faircloth Amendment, the 1998 rule that generally bars public housing agencies from building new units if it would increase their total number.
Makes public housing capital and operating funding permanent and mandatory, so agencies no longer depend on annual appropriations for upkeep and basic operations.
Authorizes $20 billion per year through FY2032 for the Housing Trust Fund to build 2.5 million affordable private-market units that must remain affordable for their entire useful life.

Creates a $200 billion Community Control and Anti-Displacement Fund for local governments to fight gentrification and neighborhood destabilization, prioritizing ownership models that give renters a say in how housing is run.

Bars discrimination based on criminal record or immigration status in the rental of units built with this assistance, and requires transit access, environmental standards, accessibility, and supportive services.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through roughly $300 billion per year in new mandatory and authorized spending — $80 billion for public housing construction, $20 billion for the Housing Trust Fund, and $200 billion total for the anti-displacement fund over FY2022–FY2032.

drawbacks.text: The spending is enormous: $80 billion and $20 billion per year for eleven fiscal years plus a $200 billion anti-displacement fund, all added on top of existing federal budgets without an identified funding source.

The construction goal of 9.5 million public units in ten years would vastly expand a national stock that today numbers around one million units, a scale of building that no comparable federal program has attempted.

The bill left the details largely to future regulation: transit siting, environmental standards, and supportive services plans were all to be defined by HUD rules, so the practical burden on local agencies and the pace of delivery were unknown.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households paying more than half their income in rent, the bill offered a direct, structural answer: publicly owned homes that stay affordable permanently. The cost — roughly $300 billion a year for a decade — was comparable in size to major national programs, and the bill offered no revenue offset. The trade-off was genuine, not cosmetic: the benefit was enormous and targeted at the poorest renters, and so was the price tag.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it went nowhere before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ilhan Omar introduced the Homes for All Act on March 21, 2022, with eight original cosponsors.
Nine House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction.
No further action appears in the bill's history: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No constituency gained housing from what happened; the bill's supporters gained nothing, and federal spending stayed at existing levels, sparing taxpayers a roughly $300-billion-a-year commitment that was never debated on its merits.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after its referral on March 21, 2022.

sides.party_line_note: All ten supporters were Democrats and none were Republicans; the bill then died in committee without any recorded vote to break down by party.

industries.note: The bill's central beneficiaries: it would have built 12 million permanently affordable units for the households most burdened by rent. Because the bill died, this group gained nothing.

Building 12 million units over a decade would have been one of the largest public construction programs in U.S. history, a large source of contracts and jobs. Its interest ran alongside renters' here.

The bill made their capital and operating funding permanent and mandatory and made them the permanent owners and operators of 9.5 million new units they are currently barred from building. Their role would have been locked in and dramatically expanded.

A large new stock of rent-capped public and permanently affordable units would compete with market-rate rentals in the same metro areas. These landlords profit from the rents the program would have undercut.
